items.stem: On a pipelined processor, what does pipelining primarily improve?

options.text: Instruction throughput, by overlapping the execution of multiple instructions
options.rationale: Correct: pipelining raises throughput; the latency of a single instruction does not fall.

options.text: The latency of a single instruction
options.rationale: A single instruction still takes at least as long; only throughput improves.

options.text: The total number of transistors required
options.rationale: Pipelining adds registers; it is about throughput, not transistor count.
Cache behaviour is separate from pipelining.

items.explanation: Correct: pipelining raises throughput; the latency of a single instruction does not fall.

items.stem: Which two situations create a pipeline hazard that may require stalling or forwarding? (Select TWO)

options.text: An instruction needs a result that an earlier, not-yet-finished instruction will produce
options.rationale: Correct: that is a data hazard (read-after-write).

options.text: A branch's outcome is not yet known when the next instruction must be fetched
options.rationale: Correct: that is a control hazard.

options.text: Two instructions use different registers with no shared data
options.rationale: Independent instructions do not create a hazard.
A no-op introduces no dependency hazard.

items.explanation: Correct: that is a data hazard (read-after-write).; Correct: that is a control hazard.

items.stem: A cache miss that occurs the very first time a block is referenced is best classified as which type?

options.rationale: Correct: the first reference to a block is a compulsory miss regardless of cache size.
Conflict misses arise from mapping collisions, not first reference.
Capacity misses arise when the working set exceeds the cache.
Coherence misses relate to multiprocessor sharing, not first reference.

items.explanation: Correct: the first reference to a block is a compulsory miss regardless of cache size.
